stem: A 38-year-old man presents with painless bright red bleeding per rectum during bowel movements. He notices prolapsed tissue that spontaneously reduces. There is no history of weight loss or change in bowel habits. What is the most appropriate management?

opts.t: Dietary fiber, stool softeners and topical analgesia

expl: Keyed: painless bleeding with prolapse that reduces spontaneously = grade II internal haemorrhoids, no red flags in a 38-year-old → start conservative (fibre, fluids, stool softeners, topical agents), the first line for every grade; rubber band ligation if symptoms persist.

why.C: Banding is the next step (the slide pairs grade II with banding) — not the first.

stem: A 20-year-old man, otherwise healthy, presented to the outpatient department complaining of per-rectal bleeding for 3 months. Anorectal examination showed 3rd degree hemorrhoids. He has a family history of Colon cancer and Symptoms of Iron deficiency anemia. Which of the following is the appropriate next step in management?
expl: Rectal bleeding with iron-deficiency anaemia and a family history of colon cancer → colonoscopy to exclude a proximal lesion before attributing bleeding to haemorrhoids.

why.A: Treating the haemorrhoids first could miss cancer.
why.B: Treating the haemorrhoids first could miss cancer.
why.C: Upper endoscopy isn't first for fresh rectal bleeding.

stem: A 55 years old male known case of crohn's diease 10 years ago. Diagnosed with complex fistula and 4-cm perianal abcese. What is the best managment option :
expl: Complex fistula + abscess in Crohn's → incision and drainage + loose (draining) seton; then medical therapy (anti-TNF). Fistulotomy of a complex Crohn's fistula risks incontinence and non-healing.

why.B: Fistulotomy is only for simple low fistulas.
why.C: Sitz baths don't drain an abscess.

stem: A patient has an anterior, posterior midline, and a lateral fissure, which of the following is the next step?
expl: Multiple fissures including a lateral one are atypical → investigate for an underlying cause (Crohn's, TB, syphilis, HIV, malignancy) — colonoscopy (± EUA and biopsy) before treating it as a simple fissure.

why.D: Sphincterotomy is dangerous if Crohn's is present.

stem: A 30 year old man with anal pain and bright blood per rectum that appears after defecation found to have left lateral fissure and skin tags, in PR exam he was found to have mild tenderness and relaxed sphincter tone. What is the appropriate management?
srcNote: (Lateral fissure-> risk of cancer) (anorectal disorders) (i think “C”. Surgical davidson’s 7th edition page 289) The source gives an uncertain alternative answer, and the repeated versions change option order and answer keys. The original wording is preserved. Other source key (Final 432 F • first list • Q3 (p. 214)): Answer: A (i think “C”. Surgical davidson’s 7th edition page 289) (anorectal disorders). In that version: C. Diltiazem cream with laxatives. Other source key (Final 432 F • first list • Q7 (p. 215)): Answer: (A, repeated question). In that version: A. Diltiazem cream and laxatives.
expl: A lateral fissure (atypical) with skin tags and a relaxed sphincter (a typical fissure has spasm) → suspect a specific cause (Crohn's, cancer, infection) → examination/biopsy under anaesthesia.

why.C: Botox treats spasm, and there is none here.
why.D: LIS for an atypical fissure with low tone risks incontinence.

stem: What grade of haemorrhoids that can be manually reduced?
expl: Goligher: grade I bleeds without prolapse; II prolapses and reduces spontaneously; III prolapses and needs manual reduction; IV is permanently prolapsed.

stem: A 20-year-old male presents with a simple low-lying anal fistula. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
expl: A simple low fistula crosses little sphincter → fistulotomy (lay open) has the highest cure rate with minimal incontinence risk.

why.D: LIFT is for transsphincteric fistulas where sphincter preservation matters.

stem: A 28-year-old male presents with severe anal pain persisting despite topical medications that were given to treat a posterior midline fissure. Clinical examination reveals anal sphincter spasm which prevents further examination. What is the treatment of choice for his patient?
expl: A chronic posterior fissure failing topical therapy → lateral internal sphincterotomy (gold standard, ~95% healing).

why.D: GTN has already failed (topical therapy given).

stem: Pt. presenting with perianal fistula what is the diagnostic modality of choice?
expl: Pelvic MRI is the imaging of choice for fistula-in-ano (complex/recurrent) — it shows the tract, extensions and sphincter relation; endoanal US is an alternative.

why.A: CT is poor for perianal anatomy.
why.B: Endoanal US is an alternative, not the choice.

stem: A 6 months old boy presented with his mother noticing a peri-anal red swelling for 2 days. On examination an 8 mm tender red swelling was noticed Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

opts.t: Warm water baths daily and re-evaluate after 7 days.
Incision and drainage with antibiotics for 5-7 days.

srcNote: (anorectal disease) Source note (Final 433 A Q41 (p. 185)): Diagnosis appears to be perianal abscess -> rx: incision and drainage + antibiotics
expl: A tender red perianal swelling in an infant = perianal abscess → incision and drainage; antibiotics are added in infants/cellulitis.

why.C: Antibiotics alone don't treat an abscess.

stem: A 27 y/o man presents to the emergency department with painful rectal bleeding. He mentioned that the pain is most severe during and immediately after defecating blood red. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?
srcNote: anal fissure is the only painful option in this scenario
expl: Painful bright red bleeding, worst during and after defecation = anal fissure (tear in the sensitive anoderm). Internal haemorrhoids are painless.

why.C: External haemorrhoids hurt when thrombosed, not with every defecation.
why.D: Tumours usually bleed painlessly with a change in bowel habit.

stem: A young male developed a fistula-in-ano with the external opening 1.5 cm (from anal verge) in the left postero-lateral position. Where is the internal opening likely to be?
expl: Goodsall's rule: an external opening posterior to the transverse anal line follows a curved tract to the posterior midline (6 o'clock).

why.A: Anterior openings within 3 cm run straight radially.
why.B: That would be a straight tract (anterior rule).

stem: A male patient presented with recurrent fistula, bloody mucus stool and tenesmus, colonoscopy showed unhealthy rectum, what is the likely diagnosis?
srcNote: , both answers counted as correct. (IBD) The source accepts both answers. Other recalls give ulcerative colitis alone; these original differences are retained. Other source key (Final 429 A Q30 (p. 282)): Answer: D (IBD). In that version: D. Ulcerative colitis. Other source key (Final 428 Q17 (p. 303)): Answer: A. In that version: A. Ulcerative colitis.
expl: The source accepted both: recurrent fistulae and an unhealthy rectum suggest Crohn's (fistulizing perianal disease), while bloody mucus and tenesmus with rectal involvement suggest UC.

why.C: IBS doesn't cause fistulae or bleeding.

stem: The following statements regarding anal fissure are true, except:

opts.t: longitudinal tear in the mucosa and skin of the anal canal
commonly situated at the lateral side of the anal canal
lateral fissures suggested specific lesions such as Ulcerative colitis or Malignancy
The chronic anal fissure can form A “sentinel “pile

expl: Fissures are usually in the posterior midline (~90%); lateral fissures suggest specific causes (Crohn's, UC, TB, syphilis, cancer). A chronic fissure forms a sentinel pile.

why.A: True — a longitudinal tear in the anoderm.

stem: Fistula that drains in the left lateral posterior side externally, where does it open internally?
expl: Goodsall's rule: a posterior external opening → curved tract → internal opening at the posterior midline.
